Bayesian Inference for Lineup Measures

Colin G. Tredoux

Tamsyn M. Naylor

2026-10-30

Source: vignettes/bayesian_inference.Rmd
bayesian_inference.Rmd

Acknowledgement. Large language models supplied by Anthropic and OpenAI were used in preparing this vignette, to assist with checking code, testing the veracity of the approaches described, and on occasion editing the text. Responsibility for the content rests with the authors.

Purpose

This vignette shows the Bayesian posterior summaries in r4lineups for lineup fairness and confidence-based eyewitness measures.

Use these functions when you want credible intervals or direct probability statements such as P(E′<6∣data)P(E' < 6 \mid data), P(F<6∣data)P(F < 6 \mid data), or P(DR>1∣data)P(DR > 1 \mid data). The examples use small posterior samples so that the vignette runs quickly during package checks; increase S for final analyses.

If you have only used frequentist methods

Most readers of this package will have been trained in the frequentist tradition, so it is worth setting out plainly what is different here. Nothing in what follows requires accepting a philosophical position; it is mainly about what question the interval answers.

The question you probably want to ask. Having measured a six-person lineup and obtained an effective size of 4.8, the natural question is: what is the probability that this lineup’s effective size is below 6? A frequentist confidence interval cannot answer that. It is a statement about the procedure — that intervals constructed this way contain the true value 95% of the time — not about this lineup. The true effective size either is or is not below 6, and frequentist probability does not attach to it.

A Bayesian credible interval does answer it. “There is a 95% probability that E′ lies between 4.1 and 5.6, given these data” is a statement about the quantity, and it is the statement most people believe they are making when they report a confidence interval.

How that is achieved. By treating the unknown quantity as having a distribution. Three steps:

  1. A prior describes what is believed before seeing the data. Here the priors are deliberately weak — alpha = 0.5 is the Jeffreys prior for proportions, which is close to saying “no lineup member is favoured, and I am not confident about that either”.
  2. The data update it through the likelihood.
  3. The result is the posterior, a full distribution for the quantity, from which any summary can be read: a median, an interval, or a direct probability such as P(E′<6)P(E' < 6).

Why the functions return draws rather than formulas. Effective size is 1/∑pi21/\sum p_i^2 — a nonlinear function of the choice probabilities. There is no tidy closed form for its posterior. Instead the functions sample S draws from the posterior of the probabilities and transform each draw. The resulting collection of S values is the posterior of E′, and any summary is computed from it. This is why S matters: too few draws and the summaries are noisy. Note that these are independent Monte Carlo draws, not MCMC, so there is no chain to check for convergence.

What you gain in practice, beyond the interpretation:

  • Bounded quantities behave properly. E′ cannot exceed lineup size and a proportion cannot be negative. Normal-theory intervals can and do run outside those bounds at small samples; a posterior on the natural scale cannot.
  • Direct probabilities. P(DR>1)P(DR > 1) is often exactly what a report needs, and is awkward to extract from a p-value.
  • Small samples degrade gracefully. With few mock witnesses the posterior becomes wide, which is the honest result, rather than producing a narrow interval resting on an asymptotic approximation that does not hold.

What it does not give you. It is not a way of getting a decisive answer from thin data. A weak prior and a small sample give a wide posterior, and that width is the finding.

library(r4lineups)

Data Shapes

The Bayesian fairness functions use mock-witness lineup choices:

  • a lineup vector, where each value is the chosen lineup position; or
  • a lineup table, where each cell is the count for one lineup position.

The Bayesian calibration function uses the standard confidence-based data frame with target_present, identification, and confidence. The SDT comparison uses summary counts: hits, misses, false alarms, and correct rejections for two conditions.

Effective Size

esize_T_bayes() fits a Dirichlet-multinomial model to the lineup choice counts and transforms each posterior draw of the choice-probability vector to Tredoux’s effective size E′E'.

data(nortje2012)

lineup_vec <- nortje2012$lineup_1
k <- max(lineup_vec, na.rm = TRUE)
lineup_tab <- table(factor(lineup_vec, levels = seq_len(k)))

set.seed(1)
esize_post <- esize_T_bayes(
  lineup_tab,
  alpha = 0.5,
  S = 1000,
  threshold = k
)

esize_post
#> Bayesian Posterior: Effective Size E' (Tredoux, 1998)
#> ------------------------------------------------
#>   k (positions): 8    N (choices): 133    S (draws): 1000
#>   Prior: Dirichlet(alpha = 0.50)
#>   Posterior mean:   5.614
#>   Posterior median: 5.624
#>   95% credible interval: [4.804, 6.355]
#>   P(E' < 8.00 | data): 1.000
#>   P(E' > 8.00 | data): 0.000
plot(esize_post)

The threshold argument makes the posterior useful for fairness benchmarks. For example, with a six-person lineup one might inspect P(E′<6∣data)P(E' < 6 \mid data) as a posterior probability that the effective size falls below nominal size.

Functional Size

func_size_bayes() models the suspect-selection rate with a beta-binomial posterior and transforms posterior draws to functional size.

set.seed(2)
func_post <- func_size_bayes(
  lineup_vec,
  target_pos = 3,
  alpha = 0.5,
  S = 1000,
  threshold = k
)

func_post
#> Bayesian Functional Size - Beta-Binomial model
#>   Prior: Jeffreys-type Beta(0.50, 0.50)
#>   n = 133, suspect IDs = 19 (rate = 0.143)
#>   Posterior mean F:   7.189
#>   Posterior median F: 6.904
#>   95% credible interval: [4.746, 10.898]
#>   P(F < 8.000 | data): 0.7480
#>   P(F > 8.000 | data): 0.2520
plot(func_post)

Diagnosticity Ratio

diag_ratio_T_bayes() models target-present and target-absent suspect-selection rates with independent beta-binomial posteriors and returns the posterior of the diagnosticity ratio.

tp_vec <- nortje2012$lineup_1
ta_vec <- nortje2012$lineup_2

set.seed(3)
diag_post <- diag_ratio_T_bayes(
  lineup_pres = tp_vec,
  lineup_abs = ta_vec,
  pos_pres = 3,
  pos_abs = 3,
  k1 = max(tp_vec, na.rm = TRUE),
  k2 = max(ta_vec, na.rm = TRUE),
  alpha = 0.5,
  S = 1000,
  threshold = 1
)

diag_post
#> Bayesian Diagnosticity Ratio (Tredoux) - Beta-Binomial model
#>   Prior: Jeffreys-type Beta(0.50, 0.50)
#>   TP lineup: n = 133, suspect IDs = 19
#>   TA lineup: n = 133, suspect IDs = 5
#>   Posterior mean DR:   4.301
#>   Posterior median DR: 3.645
#>   95% credible interval: [1.550, 11.214]
#>   P(DR < 1.000 | data): 0.0010
#>   P(DR > 1.000 | data): 0.9990
plot(diag_post)

The threshold 1 is useful because DR>1DR > 1 indicates that suspect identifications are more common in the target-present lineup than in the target-absent lineup.

Calibration

calibration_bayes() places beta posteriors on accuracy within confidence bins and propagates uncertainty into calibration CC, over/underconfidence O/UO/U, and normalized resolution NRINRI.

data(lineup_example)

set.seed(4)
cal_post <- calibration_bayes(
  lineup_example,
  confidence_bins = c(0, 60, 80, 100),
  alpha = 0.5,
  S = 1000
)

cal_post
#> Bayesian Calibration Analysis - Beta-Binomial model
#>   n = 503; 3 confidence bins; prior alpha = 0.50
#>   C (calibration):      mean = 0.0729, median = 0.0727, 95% CI [0.0545, 0.0913]
#>   O/U (over/underconf): mean = -0.2268, median = -0.2266, 95% CI [-0.2564, -0.1931]
#>   NRI (resolution):     mean = 0.0450, median = 0.0447, 95% CI [0.0216, 0.0721]
#>   (Frequentist: C = 0.0727, O/U = -0.2290, NRI = 0.0453)
plot(cal_post, metric = "C")

plot(cal_post, metric = "NRI")

SDT d’ Comparison

sdt_compare() compares two conditions using summary SDT counts. It draws from posterior hit and false-alarm rates, converts each draw to d′d', and reports the posterior for Δd′=dA′−dB′\Delta d' = d'_A - d'_B.

set.seed(5)
sdt_post <- sdt_compare(
  hits_A = 45, misses_A = 55, fas_A = 12, crs_A = 88,
  hits_B = 38, misses_B = 62, fas_B = 10, crs_B = 90,
  label_A = "Procedure A",
  label_B = "Procedure B",
  alpha = 0.5,
  S = 1000
)

sdt_post
#> Bayesian SDT Comparison: Procedure A vs Procedure B
#>   Prior: Jeffreys Beta(0.50, 0.50) on HR and FAR
#>   Posterior mean d': Procedure A = 1.042, Procedure B = 0.971
#>   Delta d' (Procedure A - Procedure B):
#>     Posterior mean:   0.072
#>     Posterior median: 0.072
#>     95% CI: [-0.505, 0.635]
#>   P(d'_Procedure A > d'_Procedure B | data): 0.6150
#>   P(d'_Procedure B > d'_Procedure A | data): 0.3850
#>   (Frequentist z-test: z = 0.254, p = 0.7994)
plot(sdt_post)

Workflow Position

These Bayesian functions complement, rather than replace, the frequentist and bootstrap functions elsewhere in the package:

  • use normal-theory functions for quick classical intervals where assumptions are acceptable;
  • use bootstrap functions when you want sampling-distribution uncertainty with minimal distributional assumptions;
  • use Bayesian functions when credible intervals and direct posterior probabilities are the clearest way to express uncertainty.

For substantive reports, run enough posterior draws for stable summaries and check sensitivity to the prior concentration, for example alpha = 0.1, 0.5, and 1.

sensitivity <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.1, 0.5, 1.0), function(a) {
  set.seed(11)
  post <- esize_T_bayes(lineup_tab, alpha = a, S = 2000, threshold = k)
  data.frame(
    `Prior alpha`      = a,
    `Posterior median` = round(post$posterior_median, 3),
    `Lower`            = round(post$credible_interval[["lower"]], 3),
    `Upper`            = round(post$credible_interval[["upper"]], 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))

knitr::kable(
  sensitivity, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Sensitivity of the E' posterior to prior concentration, nortje2012 lineup 1 (nominal size 8)."
)
Sensitivity of the E’ posterior to prior concentration, nortje2012 lineup 1 (nominal size 8).
Prior alpha Posterior median Lower Upper
0.1 5.530 4.702 6.255
0.5 5.622 4.785 6.346
1.0 5.706 4.861 6.485

If the three rows agree closely, as they generally will once there are a few dozen choices, the prior is doing little and the result is driven by the data. Disagreement is a signal that the sample is too small for the data to dominate, and should be reported rather than resolved by picking a prior.

Technical Details

What is being sampled

Function Model Transformation applied to each draw
esize_T_bayes() Dirichlet-multinomial on the k choice counts E′=1/∑ipi2E' = 1/\sum_i p_i^2
func_size_bayes() Beta-binomial on suspect selections F=1/psuspectF = 1/p_{\text{suspect}}
diag_ratio_T_bayes() Independent beta-binomials for the two lineups DR=pTP/pTADR = p_{\text{TP}} / p_{\text{TA}}
calibration_bayes() Beta posterior on accuracy within each confidence bin C, O/U and NRI
sdt_compare() Beta posteriors on hit and false-alarm rates Δd′=dA′−dB′\Delta d' = d'_A - d'_B

In each case the posterior of the transformed quantity is obtained by transforming draws, not by approximating the transformation. This matters for quantities like DRDR, a ratio whose sampling distribution is markedly skewed: the posterior inherits that skew correctly, where a symmetric normal-theory interval would not.

The prior

alpha is the concentration parameter of the Dirichlet or beta prior, applied symmetrically. alpha = 0.5 is the Jeffreys prior, alpha = 1 is uniform, and smaller values place more weight near the boundaries. All are weak; with more than a few dozen observations the likelihood dominates, which the sensitivity check above is there to confirm.

Monte Carlo error

Summaries are computed from S independent draws, so they carry Monte Carlo error of order 1/S1/\sqrt{S}. These are not Markov chains, so autocorrelation and convergence diagnostics do not apply. S = 1000 is adequate for a median, but tail probabilities and interval endpoints need more — use 10,000 or more where a reported number depends on them.

Assumptions

  1. Choices are independent across witnesses, and each witness contributes one.
  2. The Dirichlet-multinomial treats members as exchangeable a priori. That is a statement about prior ignorance, not a claim that foils are interchangeable in fact; the data are what distinguish them.
  3. diag_ratio_T_bayes() treats the two lineups as independent samples.
  4. sdt_compare() assumes equal-variance signal detection, as the classical d′d' does.

References

Agresti, A., & Agresti, B. F. (1978). Statistical analysis of qualitative variation. Sociological Methodology, 9, 204-237.

Tredoux, C. G. (1998). Statistical inference on measures of lineup fairness. Law and Human Behavior, 22(2), 217-237.
